questions.stem: Inflation is best defined as

options.text: a sustained rise in the general price level
a one-day increase in the price of petrol
a fall in the volume of money in circulation
an increase in the output of all goods

questions.explanation: Inflation is a continuing rise across a wide basket of prices, which cuts the purchasing power of the naira. A single price jump, a shrinking money supply, or a rise in output does not by itself meet that definition.

distractorRationale.b: A one-off rise in one commodity is a relative price change, not inflation, unless it spreads and persists
distractorRationale.c: A fall in the money supply is more likely to be associated with deflation
distractorRationale.d: Higher output tends to ease inflation if demand is unchanged

questions.stem: Demand-pull inflation occurs when

options.text: aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply at current prices
wages and imported input costs rise independently of demand
the government imposes a maximum price on food
the CBN sells Treasury bills on a large scale

questions.explanation: Demand-pull inflation is 'too much money chasing too few goods': planned spending is greater than what the economy can supply, so prices are bid up. Cost-push inflation, by contrast, starts from the supply side with higher wages or import prices.

distractorRationale.b: This is the description of cost-push inflation, not demand-pull
distractorRationale.c: A maximum price is a control measure and typically creates shortages rather than inflation
distractorRationale.d: Selling Treasury bills is contractionary OMO, which reduces rather than raises demand

questions.stem: A consumer price index rises from 120 in one year to 150 in the next. What is the inflation rate, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Inflation rate = (change in the index ÷ previous index) × 100. The index rose by 30 points from a previous level of 120, so 30/120 × 100 = 25 per cent. Dividing by the new index of 150 would wrongly give 20 per cent.

questions.stem: During inflation, which group is most likely to gain?

options.text: Creditors who are owed a fixed sum of naira
Pensioners on a fixed naira pension
Debtors who repay loans with depreciating naira
Savers holding cash under a mattress

questions.explanation: A debtor contracted to repay a fixed naira amount hands back money that buys less than when the loan was taken, so the real burden of the debt falls. Creditors, pensioners and cash savers receive or hold naira whose purchasing power has shrunk, so they lose.

distractorRationale.a: Creditors are paid back in weaker naira, so they lose in real terms
distractorRationale.b: A fixed pension buys fewer goods as prices rise, so pensioners lose
distractorRationale.d: Idle cash loses purchasing power at the full rate of inflation

questions.stem: Which pair of measures is appropriate for controlling demand-pull inflation?

options.text: Raising the MPR and running a budget surplus
Cutting the CRR and increasing government spending
Buying securities in OMO and cutting taxes
Printing more naira and granting cheap credit

questions.explanation: Demand-pull inflation needs a reduction in spending. A higher Monetary Policy Rate dearens credit, and a budget surplus (higher tax or lower spending) withdraws purchasing power. The other options are expansionary and would add to demand.

distractorRationale.b: A lower CRR and higher spending both expand demand and would worsen demand-pull inflation
distractorRationale.c: Buying securities injects cash, and a tax cut raises disposable income — both are expansionary
distractorRationale.d: Printing money and cheap credit are classic sources of demand-pull inflation

questions.stem: In a hypothetical basket, rice has a price relative of 125 (weight 4), beans 110 (weight 2) and oil 120 (weight 4). The weighted price index is
questions.explanation: The weighted sum of the price relatives is (125 × 4) + (110 × 2) + (120 × 4) = 500 + 220 + 480 = 1,200. Dividing by the total weight of 10 gives an index of 120. Forgetting to divide by the weights, or averaging the relatives without weights, produces the distractors.

distractorRationale.a: This is the simple (unweighted) average of 125, 110 and 120, which ignores the different weights
distractorRationale.c: This is the sum of the three price relatives with no weighting and no division
distractorRationale.d: This is the weighted sum before dividing by the total weight of 10

questions.stem: Which of the following is a type of inflation classified by cause?
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation occurs when the overall prices increase due to rising costs of wages and raw materials. This type of inflation is classified by cause, as opposed to others that may be classified by rate or other factors.

distractorRationale.b: Seasonal inflation is not a recognized type of inflation based on cause; it relates more to price changes due to seasonal demand.
distractorRationale.c: Structural inflation is not a standard classification; inflation is typically categorized into demand-pull, cost-push, and built-in inflation.
distractorRationale.d: Hyperinflation is an extreme form of inflation but is classified by rate rather than cause.

questions.stem: What is the formula for calculating the inflation rate using the Consumer Price Index (CPI)?

options.text: ((CPI current year - CPI previous year) / CPI previous year) x 100
(CPI previous year / CPI current year) x 100
CPI current year - CPI previous year

questions.explanation: The correct formula to calculate the inflation rate is ((CPI current year - CPI previous year) / CPI previous year) x 100, which provides the percentage change in the CPI over the year. This calculation helps in understanding how much prices have increased compared to the previous year.

distractorRationale.b: This formula incorrectly suggests the inverse calculation and does not yield the inflation rate.
distractorRationale.c: This option provides an average rather than a rate of inflation.
distractorRationale.d: This simply gives the change in CPI without expressing it as a percentage of the previous year's CPI.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a common effect of inflation?
questions.explanation: While inflation can lead to various economic changes, higher unemployment rates are not a direct effect of inflation. Generally, inflation can coincide with lower unemployment as businesses may hire more to meet increased demand.

distractorRationale.a: Decreased purchasing power is a direct consequence of inflation as prices rise.
distractorRationale.b: Increased cost of living is a fundamental effect of inflation, impacting daily expenses.
distractorRationale.d: Increased interest rates often occur as a response to inflation to curb spending.

questions.stem: Which of the following groups is most likely to be negatively affected by inflation?
questions.explanation: Fixed-income earners, such as retirees on pensions, are negatively affected by inflation because their income does not increase with rising prices, leading to a decline in their purchasing power. This can severely impact their ability to maintain their standard of living.

distractorRationale.b: Borrowers may benefit from inflation as they repay loans with less valuable money.
distractorRationale.c: Investors can sometimes benefit from inflation if their investments appreciate in value.
distractorRationale.d: Business owners may pass on costs to consumers, potentially maintaining their profit margins.

questions.stem: Which monetary policy tool is primarily used to control inflation?
questions.explanation: Adjusting interest rates is a primary monetary policy tool used to control inflation. By increasing interest rates, central banks can reduce spending and borrowing, which in turn can help to decrease inflationary pressures in the economy.

distractorRationale.b: Increasing government spending can actually exacerbate inflation rather than control it.
distractorRationale.c: Decreasing taxes can increase disposable income and spending, potentially worsening inflation.
distractorRationale.d: Regulating wages is not a direct monetary policy tool; it is more related to labor market policies.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a price index?

options.text: To measure changes in the price level over time
To determine the average income of consumers
To calculate the total GDP of a country
To assess employment rates in the economy

questions.explanation: The primary purpose of a price index is to measure changes in the price level over time, which helps economists and policymakers understand inflation trends and the cost of living adjustments required for consumers.

distractorRationale.b: Determining average income is not the function of a price index; it focuses on price changes.
distractorRationale.c: Calculating GDP is a separate economic metric that does not involve price indices.
distractorRationale.d: Assessing employment rates is unrelated to the function of a price index.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fiscal measure to control inflation?
questions.explanation: Increasing taxes is a fiscal measure that can help control inflation by reducing disposable income and, consequently, consumer spending. This can help to alleviate inflationary pressures in the economy.

distractorRationale.b: Decreasing interest rates is a monetary measure that could stimulate spending rather than control inflation.
distractorRationale.c: Increasing the money supply is generally associated with higher inflation, not controlling it.
distractorRationale.d: Lowering tariffs could lead to increased spending and demand, potentially worsening inflation.

questions.stem: What is built-in inflation?

options.text: Inflation resulting from rising production costs
Inflation that occurs due to adaptive expectations
Inflation that is controlled by government policies

questions.explanation: Built-in inflation occurs when businesses and workers expect prices to rise in the future, leading to wage increases and further price rises. This creates a self-perpetuating cycle of inflation driven by expectations.

distractorRationale.a: This describes cost-push inflation, not built-in inflation.
distractorRationale.b: This describes demand-pull inflation, which is different from built-in inflation.
distractorRationale.d: Built-in inflation is not directly controlled by government policies but is influenced by expectations.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a likely consequence of hyperinflation?
questions.explanation: In cases of hyperinflation, the value of currency can plummet to the point where it becomes virtually worthless, leading to a breakdown in the normal functioning of the economy. This can create severe economic instability and hardship for consumers.

distractorRationale.b: Hyperinflation is characterized by instability, not stable economic growth.
distractorRationale.c: Increased investment is unlikely during hyperinflation due to uncertainty and risk.
distractorRationale.d: Lower unemployment rates are not a typical outcome of hyperinflation; often, unemployment rises due to economic chaos.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common measure used to calculate inflation?
questions.explanation: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a common measure used to calculate inflation, as it tracks the average change in prices over time for a basket of goods and services. This is essential for understanding inflation's impact on consumers.

distractorRationale.a: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures economic output, not inflation directly.
distractorRationale.c: The Employment Rate is unrelated to the measurement of inflation.
distractorRationale.d: The Balance of Trade measures the difference between exports and imports, not inflation.

questions.stem: Cost-push inflation is primarily caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation occurs when the overall prices increase due to rising costs of production, such as wages and raw materials. This type of inflation can reduce the supply of goods and services in the economy.

distractorRationale.a: Increased consumer demand leads to demand-pull inflation, not cost-push.
distractorRationale.c: Government spending can influence demand but is not a direct cause of cost-push inflation.
distractorRationale.d: An increased money supply typically leads to demand-pull inflation rather than cost-push.

questions.stem: If the inflation rate is 8% this year, what does that imply about the purchasing power of money?
questions.explanation: An inflation rate of 8% means that the value of money decreases, and consumers can purchase 8% less than they could the previous year with the same amount of money. Therefore, purchasing power declines.

distractorRationale.a: The purchasing power does not increase during inflation; it decreases.
distractorRationale.b: The purchasing power cannot remain the same when there is inflation.
distractorRationale.d: A decrease of 16% is not accurate; it is a direct reflection of the inflation rate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a likely effect of inflation on savers?
questions.explanation: During inflation, the real value of money decreases, meaning that the purchasing power of savings diminishes. Savers effectively lose money as inflation erodes the value of their saved funds.

distractorRationale.a: Inflation typically discourages saving since the value of money decreases.
distractorRationale.c: Higher interest rates may occur but often lag behind inflation, failing to protect savers.
distractorRationale.d: Inflation can create uncertainty, which often does not lead to more investment opportunities.

questions.explanation: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is the primary measure used to track inflation by monitoring the average change over time in the prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services.

distractorRationale.a: Gross Domestic Product measures economic output, not inflation.
distractorRationale.c: The unemployment rate indicates labor market conditions, not inflation.
distractorRationale.d: The balance of payments tracks international trade and finance, not inflation.

questions.explanation: Increasing subsidies for essential goods can actually exacerbate inflation by increasing demand without addressing the underlying causes of inflation. The other options are common strategies to help control inflation.

distractorRationale.a: Increasing interest rates is a common method to control inflation by reducing borrowing.
distractorRationale.b: Reducing government spending can help lower inflation by decreasing demand.
distractorRationale.c: Increasing taxes can reduce disposable income and thus decrease spending, helping control inflation.

questions.stem: What is hyperinflation?

options.text: Inflation at a rate of 10% or more
Inflation that occurs during a recession

questions.explanation: Hyperinflation refers to extremely high and typically accelerating rates of inflation, often exceeding 50% per month. It can lead to a loss of confidence in the currency and severe economic instability.

distractorRationale.a: 10% inflation is significant but does not qualify as hyperinflation.
distractorRationale.c: A stable price level indicates no inflation, which is the opposite of hyperinflation.
distractorRationale.d: Inflation during a recession is not defined as hyperinflation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a consequence of inflation for borrowers?
questions.explanation: For borrowers, inflation can decrease the real cost of debt because they repay loans with money that has less purchasing power. This can make borrowing more attractive during inflationary periods.

distractorRationale.a: The burden of debt may decrease in real terms during inflation.
distractorRationale.c: Higher interest rates may occur but are not a direct consequence of inflation for borrowers.
distractorRationale.d: Lower borrowing costs are not typically a result of inflation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes stagflation?
questions.explanation: Stagflation is an economic condition characterized by high inflation combined with high unemployment and stagnant demand. It presents a unique challenge for policymakers.

distractorRationale.a: High inflation typically correlates with low unemployment, not stagflation.
distractorRationale.c: Low inflation and high growth indicate a healthy economy, not stagflation.
distractorRationale.d: Low inflation and low growth do not reflect the inflationary pressures seen in stagflation.
